sources.title: Chakraborty et al. (2014), Mixed Fortunes: Ancient Expansion and Recent Decline in Population Size of a Subtropical Montane Primate, the Arunachal Macaque Macaca munzala
sources.version: PLOS ONE 9(7):e97061; version of record published 2014-07-23. A linked 2014-12-17 correction concerns Figure S1's map, not the demographic results cited here.
sources.locator: Abstract and citation (lines 131-140); population sampling (lines 163-175); approximate Bayesian computation methods (lines 187-220); Results, Upper Subansiri Scenario 2 and effective population-size estimates (lines 243-266); sampling/migration and causal limitations (lines 225-229 and 319-327); linked correction notice (lines 112-114).
sources.license: The PLOS article copyright statement links to the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 license.
sources.scope: Original population-genetic study using mitochondrial DNA and microsatellite data from three tentative Arunachal macaque populations; the claim is limited to the Upper Subansiri sample and its model-based demographic inference.
sources.rightsHolder: Chakraborty, Sinha, and Ramakrishnan, as identified in the article.
sources.licenseEvidenceLocator: PLOS copyright statement at lines 140-141 identifies an open-access Creative Commons Attribution license and links to the CC BY 4.0 deed.
sources.licenseAppliesTo: Published article text; this dossier paraphrases reported model estimates and does not reproduce tables or figures.
sources.attribution: Chakraborty D, Sinha A, Ramakrishnan U. (2014). Mixed Fortunes: Ancient Expansion and Recent Decline in Population Size of a Subtropical Montane Primate, the Arunachal Macaque Macaca munzala. PLoS ONE 9(7):e97061. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0097061. Findings paraphrased.

claims.text: In the study's approximate Bayesian computation analysis, decline Scenario 2 was the best fit for the tentative Upper Subansiri population. The model estimated effective population size fell from approximately 50,600 macaques (95% HPD 19,600-68,300) to approximately 1,700 (95% HPD 476-4,090), about a 30-fold decline, around 3,500 years before present (95% HPD 520-13,800). This is a model-based historical effective-population estimate for one sampled population, not a census or a species-wide reconstruction; the study could not rule out unsampled migration and did not establish whether climate or human activity caused the inferred decline.
claims.locator: Results, Approximate Bayesian Computation approach (lines 243-266); Upper Subansiri sample and population definitions (lines 167-175); uncertainty on unsampled migrants (lines 225-229); causal and small-sample limitations (lines 319-327).
claims.placeTimeScope: Upper Subansiri, Arunachal Pradesh, northeastern India; 2014 publication. The tentative population was sampled through dried skin from old hunting trophies; 10 Upper Subansiri individuals were successfully sequenced from the original 12 samples. The estimate concerns the modeled historical effective population size, with the reported decline centered near 3,500 years before present.
claims.lifeStatus: Historical demographic inference from genotypes of sampled wild animals; one captive Tawang blood sample occurred in the wider study but not in this Upper Subansiri analysis.

claims.text: The mitochondrial-DNA Bayesian skyline plot for the tentative Upper Subansiri population indicated expansion after the Last Glacial Maximum, around 15,000 years before present. This is a model-inferred trajectory for one geographically distinct population, based on 10 successfully sequenced individuals from 12 Upper Subansiri trophy-skin samples; the study could not rule out effects of local migrants. It does not estimate census size or establish a species-wide history. The same plot's small apparent reduction 5,000–7,000 years ago may fall within the credibility interval and was not treated as conclusive evidence of a demographic shift.
claims.textZh: 基于线粒体 DNA 的贝叶斯天际线图显示，Upper Subansiri 暂定种群在末次盛冰期之后、约 15,000 年前出现扩张。这是对一个地理上独立种群的模型推断；Upper Subansiri 的 12 份旧狩猎战利品皮样本中有 10 份成功测序，研究也无法排除局部迁入者对结果的影响。该结果不估算普查数量，也不能外推为整个物种的种群史。同一图中 5,000–7,000 年前轻微下降可能位于可信区间内，因此不能视为确定的人口变化证据。
claims.locator: Bayesian skyline plot methods and results (article lines 177-182 and 224-236); sample size and successful sequencing (lines 167-175); geographically distinct populations and unsampled-migration limitation (lines 225-229); caution about interpreting the later small reduction (lines 228-229).
claims.placeTimeScope: Tentative Upper Subansiri population, Arunachal Pradesh, northeastern India; mitochondrial-DNA Bayesian skyline analysis published in 2014. Ten individuals were successfully sequenced from 12 trophy-skin samples for that population.
claims.lifeStatus: Historical demographic inference from mtDNA of sampled wild animals whose skins came from old hunting trophies; the wider study's captive Tawang blood sample is outside this Upper Subansiri claim.

gaps: The reported Bayesian estimate concerns one tentative genetic population and does not measure current census size or all populations of the species.
Local migration between sampled populations could not be ruled out; the study did not conclusively attribute the inferred decline to climate or human activity.
Morphology, life history, other ecology, current range-wide distribution, fossils, conservation status, systematic evidence search, and expert review remain unassessed.

reasons: Two model-based demographic results in one study concern the tentative Upper Subansiri population; neither estimates present-day census size or the demographic history of the full species range.

The mtDNA skyline expansion near 15,000 years before present and the separate microsatellite ABC decline estimate near 3,500 years before present depend on limited samples and do not resolve unsampled migration or causal drivers.
Morphology, life history, other ecology, range-wide distribution, fossils, conservation status, systematic evidence search, and external expert review remain unassessed.

Vocal fingerprinting reveals a substantially smaller global population of the Critically Endangered cao vit gibbon (Nomascus nasutus) than previously thought. Scientific Reports 14:416. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-023-50838-2. Findings paraphrased.

claims.text: A 2021 survey of the Cao Vit-Trung Khanh transboundary forest block combined vocal fingerprinting, field observations, and long-term monitoring records to estimate 74 individuals in 11 identified family groups of Nomascus nasutus. The authors attributed a 38% difference from an older estimate mainly to duplicate group counts in the earlier triangulation survey and reported no evidence of population decline. This is a site-specific estimate that excludes an unknown number of solitary dispersers and is not a census of the species across its former range.
claims.locator: Table 2 caption (2021 September-October acoustic sampling and exclusion of solitary dispersers); Results, Population size estimation (Par32, 11 groups and 74 individuals); Discussion (Par34, 38% difference and no evidence of decline); limitations on solitary dispersers (Par39).
claims.placeTimeScope: Cao Vit Gibbon Species and Habitat Conservation Area, Vietnam, and Bangliang Nature Reserve, China, within the Cao Vit-Trung Khanh forest block; acoustic data collected September-October 2021 at 29 listening points, interpreted alongside field observations and longer-term monitoring.
claims.lifeStatus: Free-ranging wild gibbons in protected transboundary forest; the estimate is based on identified family groups and does not include an unknown number of solitary dispersers.

gaps: The estimate covers the single known transboundary remnant forest block and omits an unknown number of solitary dispersers.
A 2021 estimate and comparison with older methods do not establish abundance across former range or long-term global trend.
Morphology, life history, other ecology, evolution, distribution beyond this survey block, fossils, conservation status beyond the cited study, systematic search, and expert review remain unassessed.

reasons: One local survey and monitoring estimate supports a bounded population claim for the Cao Vit-Trung Khanh remnant forest block.
The result excludes solitary dispersers and does not establish a global census or trend.
Most biological facets, systematic evidence search, and external expert review remain unassessed.

claims.text: Across 75 prey-presentation trials involving 22 adult rescued greater slow lorises, the study recorded brachial-gland licking five times; four observations occurred during grooming. In the only non-grooming instance, a male approached a caterpillar, withdrew to a perch, and licked its brachial gland without attempting to capture the caterpillar. This describes one captive rescue-center sample and experimental setting and does not establish how wild slow lorises use venom during prey capture.
claims.locator: Results §3.2, first paragraph, and Figure 2/caption for the five observations, grooming context, and caterpillar trial; Methods §§2.1 and 2.3 for the study subjects and 75 prey-presentation trials; limitations in Methods §2.3 and Discussion §4.1.
claims.placeTimeScope: Cikananga Wildlife Center (PPSC), West Java, Indonesia; 22 adults (11 male, 11 female) admitted in October 2013 after wild capture and confiscation; 75 home-cage prey trials conducted February-April 2014. Hunger was not controlled and the trials were not field observations.
claims.lifeStatus: Originally wild-caught, confiscated adults housed in a wildlife rescue center during artificial home-cage trials; this is not evidence of free-ranging behavior.

gaps: The claim describes rescued adults in one center and an artificial prey-presentation setup, not natural prey capture in the wild.
The authors note limitations affecting motivation and prey behavior; the observations do not establish the general function of venom use across populations.
Morphology, life history, evolution, distribution, fossils, conservation, systematic evidence search, and expert review remain unassessed.

reasons: One experimental behavior result supports a narrow claim for rescued greater slow lorises in captive prey trials.
The study does not establish natural behavior or a species-wide venom-use pattern.
Most biological facets, systematic evidence search, and external expert review remain unassessed.
